title_original: Planches Contact Festival 2026 : Cristina de Middel in Cherbourg
excerpt_original: Planches Contact Festival has invited Cristina de Middel to revisit Generation X, a project initiated by the founders of Magnum Photo Cet article Planches Contact Festival 2026 : Cristina de Middel in Cherbourg est apparu en premier sur The Eye of Photography Magazine .

blocks.text: For its 17th edition, devoted to the theme of “Generations”, the Planches Contact Festival has invited Cristina de Middel to revisit Generation X , a project initiated by the founders of Magnum Photos. With Les Atomiques de Cherbourg , the photographer turns her attention to a generation of young people trained to work in the nuclear industry. The exhibition is on view at Le Point de Vue in Deauville until January 3, 2027.

“I grew up in France. Back in the VHS days, we probably had only five or six films at home that we watched over and over again. One of them was The Umbrellas of Cherbourg . I still know the songs and dialogue by heart,” recalls Cristina de Middel.

So when Giulietta Palumbo, Editorial Director at Magnum Photos, suggested that she explore a more documentary approach to Normandy for her residency at the Planches Contact Festival, the photographer and former president of the agency decided to focus on Cherbourg, on the Cotentin Peninsula. Instead of the colours and songs of Jacques Demy’s film, however, she discovered a very different reality: a nuclear industry recruiting an entire generation of young people.
A generation confident about its future

In Cherbourg, Cristina de Middel made a discovery that surprised her. “There is a striking contrast between the young people in this town and those I know,” the photographer explains. “They are able to plan their futures in astonishing detail. They know exactly how much they will earn next year, in five years, in ten years, in fifteen years. They are entering a career that is strongly supported by the government, so everything is mapped out. There is no uncertainty.”

Generation Z is often associated with disillusioned and angry young people. In the Cotentin Peninsula, a major centre of France’s nuclear industry, the photographer captures a different side of this generation: young people who are satisfied with and proud of working in the nuclear sector. Here, everything is designed to encourage young people to pursue careers in the industry. In front of the camera, they readily pose in their uniforms.

By placing them in settings reminiscent of The Umbrellas of Cherbourg and using the same colour palette as the film, Cristina de Middel establishes a connection between two eras, and between fiction and reality.

“I wanted to give my images an early twentieth-century appearance, to portray these young people today as we might have portrayed our grandparents, who knew that if they studied, they would get a job, then have a family, then go on holidays. Everything depended on personal effort rather than external circumstances,” she explains.

She also draws a parallel between two lives shaped by the state: in Demy’s film, the protagonist is sent to fight in the Algerian War; today, the state encourages young people to enter the nuclear industry, in which it is investing heavily.

Through Les Atomiques de Cherbourg , the photographer raises several questions: “What if the state invested in less controversial industries? To what extent does it have the power to control our lives, our futures and our quality of life?”

With Les Atomiques de Cherbourg , Cristina de Middel continues an ambitious project initiated by the founders of Magnum Photos. In the postwar years, eleven photographers from the agency set out to document young people around the world. Initiated by Robert Capa in 1951, the Generation X project involved meeting people aged between twenty and twenty-five and asking them about their everyday lives. Presented at the Planches Contact Festival in dialogue with de Middel’s work, it provides the starting point for the 17th edition’s exploration of the theme.
For the photographer, this dialogue with the archives is particularly valuable. “On a personal level, it is interesting to discover Magnum archives that I myself had never seen before,” she explains.

She identifies recurring “cycles” that photography helps reveal, with young people continually facing difficult choices. “Without these archives, without this reference point, what I did in Cherbourg would have much less depth,” the artist continues.

She also considers it an honour to add a chapter to a project that marked the beginning of a collaborative way of working distinctive to Magnum Photos. “This chorus of different voices and different approaches can only help build a vision of the world in all its complexity,” concludes Cristina de Middel.
